paragraph.text: 1. How is this different from normal FS25 livestock?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Normal livestock can feel like supplying a building with feed and waiting for products. F2M inherits Realistic Livestock's individual-animal system. Choosing a calf, planning a mating, keeping breeding stock, selecting feed, deciding when to stop finishing, and choosing live sale or contract slaughter all become meaningful decisions.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Realism does not mean copying every real-world number directly into the game. Growth periods, dry matter, dressing percentages and market prices guide calibration. The model must also accommodate one-day game months, storage in liters and map production chains that settle in generic product units. Compare the costs and benefits of your choices, rather than focusing on one price or weight.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 2. A recommended first session
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: 1. Enable F2M in a new save, or back up an existing save first. Hof Bergmann is a suitable first map.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 2. Open the RL Menu with the default Right Shift + O. Alternatively, select a pen on the ESC Animals page and use its Manage animals action (usually R at this documentation baseline). Bindings can be changed.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 3. Open Info / Manage, choose a pen and an animal, and identify the pen summary on the left and individual details on the right.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 4. Compare two animals of the same breed: one with stronger meat genetics and another with stronger milk genetics. Also compare age, weight, condition and sale price.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 5. Start with Legacy feeding. Later, try Real-equivalent nutrition and examine dry-matter shares, energy and predicted feed consumption in the Ration window.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 6. Name or mark animals and try a saved filter. Learn the rules before allowing the Herdsman to buy, sell or move animals automatically.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 7. Before selling, compare a live sale with the net return from slaughter and meat sales. Comparing gross receipts alone is misleading.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 3. Game months, model time and liters per day
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Game month / period: animal ages increase in months. Many growth, input/output and price curves use periods. This unit appears in ages, milk curves, monitoring and pricing.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Game days and hours: your days-per-month setting determines the calendar schedule. Scripts update feeding, health and other state hourly or daily.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Model day: Real-equivalent nutrition treats one game month as 30 model days and divides calculations into steps. This is the basis of kg DM/head/day, energy requirements and ration budgets.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Many animal-page input/output quantities are expressed per game month. In Real-equivalent mode, kg/d refers to each animal's daily dry-matter intake in the model, not necessarily the kilograms consumed during 24 hours of game time. Changing days per month should not simply multiply monthly economic results by that number of days.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 4. Animal-list cards
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Cards help you choose an animal. They may show its image, breed or name, identity number, price and disease, pregnancy or birth-related icons. Marks and icons are useful aids; price alone does not establish quality.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Read breed, sex and age first, then the price and important status icons. Open the details to inspect genetics, production, health and weight. In breeding groups, first rule out animals that cannot breed or are ill.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Names are not identities. Unique ID identifies the individual. Farm ID, origin and ear-tag information support registration and ownership; pedigree links use identities too. Renaming an animal does not make two animals the same individual.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 5. Left side: Pen / Husbandry information
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Most figures on the left describe the entire pen, rather than the selected animal.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Animals / Capacity: current head count and facility capacity. Leave room for births and purchases; a full pen can block transactions or prevent offspring from remaining there.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Food / Food total: feed in storage plus applicable meadow resources. This is inventory, not proof of a balanced ration.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Food bar: the filled proportion of feed-storage capacity. A full trough does not prove adequate protein, fiber or water.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Food months: estimated months of supply based on current head count and consumption. Purchases, growth and pregnancy change the estimate.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: (<1d) / (<2d): a warning that feed may last less than one or two game days, not one or two model days. Refill promptly.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Condition: base-game water, bedding and other pen requirements. These can affect health, production or normal operation.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Meadow: available pasture resources normally contribute to food totals, but are seasonal. Summer supplies do not establish winter carrying capacity.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Food total can include meadow resources while a particular capacity bar measures only trough/storage fill. A nonzero total with a relatively empty storage bar is therefore not necessarily an error.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 5.1 Additional body-condition summary [Default; supported animals only]
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Avg. BCS: the average condition of applicable females. It shows whether the herd is losing or gaining reserves, but averages hide extremes.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Cows thin / fat: numbers of under- and over-conditioned cows, for example 2 / 1. Find those individuals; this is not a count of poor and good genetics.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Bulls ready: animals meeting the code's finishing criteria, such as 3 / 8. This is more useful than applying one sale-age threshold to every bull.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Bulls overfat: males beyond the preferred finishing condition. Check whether waiting longer is already counterproductive.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Feed eaten: actual feed eaten in the previous feeding step as a proportion of demand. It helps identify shortages or feed that the current model will not consume.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Ration energy: how much of that step's energy requirement the actual intake supplied. Eating enough liters is not the same as obtaining enough energy.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Water cover: water availability relative to requirements. Pay particular attention in lactating groups.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Example: Bulls ready 3/8 and Bulls overfat 1 does not mean the other four will all become more valuable. Some may be too light, insufficiently finished or too young. Read each animal's Slaughter assessment.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 5.2 Additional Real-equivalent pen readings [Opt-in]
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: These appear when the mode is enabled and the pen actually supports it.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Feed model: the active model, or the reason the pen remains on Legacy rules.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Ration target: the feeding objective and concentrate choice, for example Finishing / Auto grain.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: ME plan covered: the metabolic-energy budget coverage. 83% means about 83% of the step's planned requirement, not 83% full feed storage.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: First to run out: the ingredient predicted to be exhausted first. It does not mean every feed will run out together.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Calves on milk: warnings about inadequate milk or milk-replacer supplies for dependent calves.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Legacy mode, No supported trough, Unsupported animal or Calf on milk: dam/calf pen means you should not assume the Real-equivalent ration planner is active. See the feeding chapter for the conditions.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 6. Right side: individual information
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: The wider right pane contains the animal image, basic readings, relatives, genetics, diseases and, when monitored, input/output statistics.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Some readings are always visible; others require a monitor. This is intentional. Exact numerical information is partly gated by monitoring, whereas visibly assessable BCS and finishing condition remain available. Dealer purchase previews expose more complete information to support buying decisions.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 6.1 Individual readings
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Age: months, sometimes formatted as years and months. Always visible. Age affects breeding and slaughter eligibility; equal age does not imply equal weight.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Health: current 0-100% health. Usually requires monitoring for owned animals; purchase previews expose it. Do not confuse it with genetic Health.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Reproduction: a percentage or restriction reason for an applicable animal. It describes current progress, status or eligibility, affected by age, health, suitable males and postpartum recovery. It is not automatically the chance of pregnancy at the next mating.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Weight: current kg / adult target kg. Usually monitoring-gated for owned animals and visible in dealer previews. The denominator is not the slaughterhouse's required weight.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Finish: a 0-100 score, grade and trend for supported males. It summarizes reserves and finishing condition. A score of 100 is not the ideal endpoint.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Condition / BCS: a 1.0-5.0 score, grade and trend for supported females. Thin and fat conditions have different costs; BCS 4.5 does not mean 90% health.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Slaughter: a text assessment for applicable finishing animals, combining age, reference weight, condition and sale eligibility. Weight alone does not guarantee Ready.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Finish weight: current kg / finishing-reference kg. This measures progress toward a commercial finishing reference, unlike adult Target weight.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Ration cover: the proportion of requirements met by the actual ration when an energy budget is available. It is not the proportion of feed left in a container.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Milk output: actual output relative to the animal's current milk potential when the applicable nutrition budget exists. It is not milk already stored or sold.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Fertility (BCS): the body-condition multiplier applied to conception for applicable females. 100% means no extra condition penalty, not guaranteed pregnancy.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Pregnant: Yes / No for a female's current pregnancy. It is distinct from lactation and eligibility to mate again.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Expecting: recorded expected offspring count, not guaranteed surviving offspring.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Expected: the expected birth date, not the dealer purchase date.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Lactating: whether an applicable female is producing milk or nursing, often monitoring-gated. Yes does not guarantee spare milk available for sale.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Pedigree: parent IDs and offspring counts. Unknown parents do not mean an animal has no genetic traits.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Genetics: a 0-99 display score and grade for inherited traits. It is not a percentage or immediate production quantity.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Inputs / Outputs: monitored individual resource quantities per game month, not per real-world day or the whole pen's total.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Disease: infection, recovery, immunity, vaccination or carrier records when enabled and visible. A hidden infection may have no icon.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Value: current currency valuation, affected by breed, age, genetics, weight, condition and market. It is not net profit after transport and all historic costs.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 6.2 Reading a fictional example [Example]
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: An Angus finishing bull might show: Age 19 months; Health 94%; Weight 585.00 / 1000.00 kg; Finish 72 (moderate) +; Slaughter Ready; Finish weight 585 / 600 kg; Ration cover 100%; Overall genetics 64 - Good; Meat genetics 78 - High. Genetic numbers are illustrative too.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 1. Nineteen months is its current age; this does not itself establish how many months remain before sale.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 2. Health 94% describes current condition, not a genetic score. Check whether it is falling and why.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 3. Weight 585/1000 means it has not reached its adult target. It need not be fed all the way to 1000 kg before slaughter.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 4. Finish weight 585/600 is the relevant commercial reference. At the usual 95% threshold, roughly 570 kg satisfies the weight component.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 5. Finish 72 is in the moderate range. The + indicates rising reserves. With age and sale conditions also satisfied, the result is Ready.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 6. More feeding might add weight, but costs feed and can produce overfatness. More weight does not guarantee more profit.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 7. Meat genetics can improve yield or value, but a displayed 78 does not mean a 78% dressing percentage.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: These are teaching values, not a measured screenshot. Actual references depend on breed, individual traits, configuration and compatibility mods.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 7. What does a Monitor do?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Monitoring is a management investment in more precise information, rather than a prerequisite for animal health. Exact health, weight, parts of lactation state and individual input/output data can require it. Dealer previews expose more complete data. BCS and finishing assessments represent observable condition and do not require a purchased monitor.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Prioritize key sires, core dairy cows and animals whose finishing progress you need to track. Consider whole-herd monitoring only after allowing for its cost.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Removed monitors can leave historical records. Historical statistics are not evidence of continuing live monitoring. Follow the current button and status information.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 8. Where do the 0-99 genetic scores come from?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Ordinary internal genetic coefficients are usually around 0.25-1.75, with 1.00 the neutral average. The interface converts them to integers: Display score = round((coefficient - 0.25) / 1.50 * 99).
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Approximate pairs: 0 -> 0.25, near the minimum; 17 -> 0.50, well below average; 33 -> 0.75, somewhat below average; 50 -> 1.00, neutral; 66 -> 1.25, above average; 83 -> 1.50, well above average; 99 -> 1.75, near the maximum.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Milk 75 is not 75 liters per day. Fertility 80 is not an 80% conception chance. It places the inherited coefficient within its allowed range. Age, breed, health, condition and feeding still determine the final outcome.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Some infertile/castrated individuals use the special underlying Fertility value 0, below the normal 0.25 minimum. The display can also show 0; read Infertile as well. Complete infertility is different from merely weak fertility genetics.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 9. Five traits and Overall
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Metabolism: growth and intake tendencies. Higher values can favor growth and frame, but often increase intake and maintenance costs too. Relevant to commercial beef, finishing pigs and feed-cost decisions.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Health: inherited influences on health loss, recovery and resilience. It is not current health. Relevant to all retained breeding animals.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Fertility: affects natural breeding, AI and, for some species, litter potential. The special zero value means infertility. Relevant to sires and breeding females.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Quality / Meat (internal key quality): affects meat-related value and slaughter-model output, and contributes to live valuation. Relevant to beef animals, finishing pigs, lambs and culls.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Productivity: species-specific output, generally milk in cattle, wool in sheep, milk in goats and eggs in chickens.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Overall: a simple average of the traits an animal actually has, followed by a general rating. Useful for initial comparisons, rather than a purpose-specific breeding index.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: High Metabolism is not automatically better feed efficiency. Faster-growing animals may eat more. Commercial efficiency depends on feed and time per unit of gain.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Overall is not weighted for dairy profit or total breeding value. An Overall 80 cow with Milk 25 may be less suitable for a dairy than an Overall 65 cow with Milk 90.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 10. How are verbal grades assigned?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: 10.1 Individual grades in RLGenetics.lua compare the underlying coefficient, not the displayed integer: >=1.65 Extremely High; 1.40 to <1.65 Very High; 1.10 to <1.40 High; 0.90 to <1.10 Average; 0.70 to <0.90 Low; 0.35 to <0.70 Very Low; <0.35 Extremely Low. The special Fertility coefficient 0 is Infertile.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 10.2 Overall uses another scale. The mean coefficient is divided by the maximum 1.75, then graded: >=0.95 Extremely Good; >=0.80 Very Good; >=0.60 Good; >=0.40 Average; >=0.20 Bad; >=0.05 Very Bad; <0.05 Extremely Bad.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: A mean coefficient of 1.00 divided by 1.75 is about 0.571, so an Average overall rating is expected. Do not apply individual-trait High thresholds to Overall.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 11. Inheritance and selecting replacements
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Offspring inherit from both parents with random variation. Strong parents improve the odds of strong offspring; they do not guarantee them.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Dairy breeding: prioritize milk, then fertility and health. A high-milk cow that repeatedly loses condition or fails to conceive may still be a poor core animal.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Beef sires: consider meat, fertility, health and the value of passing traits to offspring, rather than only the sire's own meat kilograms.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Commercial finishing: consider purchase price, actual gain, meat genetics, current finish and feed costs. Fertility may not drive the profit of a bull intended for slaughter.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Sheep: balance reproduction, ewe wool and lamb sales/finishing. One exceptional trait does not remove seasonal feed costs.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 11.1 CVM in cattle
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: CVM (Complex Vertebral Malformation) is inherited rather than an ordinary contagious disease. Simplified recessive outcomes: Non-carrier x non-carrier: non-carrier offspring. Carrier x non-carrier: about 50% carriers and 50% non-carriers, without two-copy affected offspring in this simplified model. Carrier x carrier: about 25% non-carriers, 50% carriers and 25% affected offspring.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Carriers may appear healthy and can have milk-related economic incentives, but mating two carriers creates a clear offspring risk. The disease settings and CVM toggle determine whether this system is active.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 12. Breeding value is different from meat value [Cattle economics]
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: The enabled breedingValue.xml model considers future economic contributions as well as a meat-value floor. For females this includes remaining milk, reproduction and offspring value; for sires it includes the potential value of inherited traits in offspring.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Castrated, completely infertile or reproductively over-age males lose the main sire-premium logic and move closer to meat valuation. This is a live-price model. It does not automatically increase slaughter kilograms or the market price of beef.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Two equally heavy adult bulls can have very different live prices if one is a valuable sire and the other is ordinary or castrated. That price difference does not imply proportionally more beef.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 13. Adult weight and finishing weight
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: A mature breeding bull can become very large, but commercial cattle are usually sold earlier. F2M distinguishes at least three weights.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Live weight: the animal's current actual state, used for growth, loading, valuation and meat output.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Adult Target weight: mature frame potential, influenced by breed, sex and individual genetics. It is not a slaughter requirement.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Finish reference: adult target multiplied by breed/sex slaughter maturity and other applicable factors. This is the commercial finishing comparison.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Example: a 1000 kg adult target and 0.60 maturity factor produce a 600 kg finishing reference. At 590 kg, the animal is 59% of adult target but about 98% of its finishing reference. These do not conflict.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Bull maturity factors differ by breed, including Holstein, Angus, Limousin, Highland and buffalo. Two 600 kg animals may therefore be at different finishing stages. Individual targets can also depend on metabolism/frame genetics.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 13.1 Growth curves
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: The newer cattle model does not add one fixed monthly gain to every breed. weightProfiles.xml defines age-related male and female growth points. Birth weight, sex, individual development, castration, nutrition and reserves participate in the calculation.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Being 50 kg below a reference curve does not mean one extra month of feeding will necessarily recover it. Compensatory growth depends on remaining growth time and nutrition. Regular weighing and records are more reliable than adding TMR only just before slaughter.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Some parameters were derived from literature and design goals; some breeds are explicitly marked as awaiting renewed live testing. Treat these as game-model parameters, not universal standards for real farms.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 14. Finish: interpreting 0-100 [Default; mainly cattle]
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Finish is neither percentage of target weight nor a meat-genetics score. It is a changing measure of reserves and finishing condition.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: <50 lean: low reserves. Check health and nutrition rather than slaughtering on age alone. 50 to <65 store: not fully finished. Further feeding may pay, subject to costs. 65-80 moderate: the preferred condition band, provided weight and age also qualify. >80-90 fat: extra feed may not add proportionate saleable value. >90 overfat: yield conversion and some valuations may be penalized.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Moderate is a band, not a claim that exactly 72 is optimal. Aim for eligible condition and a sensible economic endpoint, rather than a perfect score.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 14.1 Trend symbols
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: + means reserves have recently been rising. - means reserves have recently been falling. No symbol means little recent change, not permanent stability.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Finish 78 (moderate) + is near the upper end of the preferred band. If weight qualifies, consider sale before it becomes fat. Finish 62 (store) - calls for checking feed quality, actual intake, water and illness.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 14.2 Finish and meat output
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: The slaughter model uses a condition-related yield multiplier. A suitable condition can have a multiplier of 1; excess fat can make some added live weight less efficiently convertible into saleable products. Live-weight value can also receive a condition adjustment. A cow's breeding and milk value should not be equated to a bull's meat finish.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Do not multiply meat price directly by the Finish score. Finish 72 does not mean 72% price, and Finish 100 does not mean 100% meat yield.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 15. Female BCS: 1-5 [Default; mainly cattle]
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Body Condition Score describes reserves in a way similar to practical visual or hands-on condition assessment. It changes with management; it is not an inherited score.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: <2.5 thin: especially concerning during peak lactation or preparation for breeding. 2.5-3.25 good: the model's suitable band, with little/no condition penalty to conception. >3.25-4.0 fleshy: more reserves; not necessarily a problem, but watch breeding performance. >4.0 fat: potentially poorer conception and unnecessary feed costs.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Example: BCS 2.7 - is still in the suitable band but is declining. At peak lactation, check whether milk is being supported by body reserves and whether the ration needs improvement before BCS falls below 2.5.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 15.1 Why reserves affect milk and breeding
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Early-lactation demand can exceed short-term energy intake. The reserve-budget model allows a cow to mobilize stored reserves to support milk, rather than generating output indefinitely at an unchanged body state.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: After peak production, with adequate feed or during the dry period, reserves can recover. Persistent underfeeding can reduce milk and conception; overfatness can also penalize reproduction. Manage the full lactation-dry-breeding cycle, rather than maintaining maximum BCS all year.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 15.2 Fertility (BCS) is not pregnancy probability
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: A 75% reading means the conception calculation formed from genetics, disease and other factors receives an approximately 0.75 condition multiplier. It does not mean a direct 75% pregnancy chance.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Rapid reserve loss can add a penalty. Animals outside the applicable system do not show this field. 100% means no extra condition penalty, not guaranteed conception.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 16. Why sufficient weight may still not mean Ready
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: The assessment checks at least sale eligibility, minimum slaughter age, overfatness, and whether both weight and condition qualify. Weight normally needs to reach 95% of the finishing reference and Finish must be at least 65.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Cannot be sold: resolve a sale restriction first. Too young: below the minimum age; keep rearing rather than bypassing a facility rule. Overfat, past best: consider selling promptly; additional fat may not pay. Ready: compare live sale against net slaughter return. Needs finishing: weight qualifies but reserves/finish do not; improve energy supply. Still growing: finish qualifies but weight does not; allow growth while watching costs. Growing: neither weight nor finish qualifies; continue rearing or sell as a store animal.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Read Slaughter first, check age and eligibility, then Finish weight, Finish, feed costs and meat prices before deciding.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 17. Castration: a business choice
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Castrated males cannot remain normal breeding sires. Some inherited rules grant growth or commercial-price benefits, while the newer cattle valuation removes sire-genetic premiums.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: It may suit non-breeding finishing stock. For an exceptional sire, the lost genetic contribution can be valuable. Do not castrate all high-genetic bulls merely because some finishing rules reward it.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Species and valuation models differ. Examine the current valuation and use a comparison save before irreversible management of expensive breeding stock.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 18. Distinguish the two feeding systems
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Legacy [Default]: new saves use the map's feed-group priorities and food-production weights, mostly expressed through game volumes and animal curves. Newly registered grain groups are not consumed under these rules. It has broader compatibility and uses inherited/map calf rules, without the same pen-level ration controls.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Real-equivalent [Opt-in]: choose it under RL Settings / Nutrition Model. It plans dry matter, energy, protein, fiber and concentrate adaptation; converts model requirements into game liters; and derives nutrients from actual feed removed. Grain can supply concentrates subject to limits. It supports AUTO / FINISH / GROW / MAINTAIN objectives and concentrate targets. Every animal in a pen must qualify, otherwise the pen falls back. Calves have additional milk and solid-feed requirements.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Selecting Real-equivalent globally does not prove it is active in every pen. Mixed unsupported animals or an unsupported trough can keep a pen on Legacy; inspect Feed model and the reason shown.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 19. Different feeds still matter in Legacy
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Grass, hay, silage and TMR are not interchangeable. Growth considers the map's food-production weights and breed forage-use coefficients. TMR generally supports faster finishing; forage types and breed utilization differ.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: For example, Highlands are more suited to extensive grass-based conditions, while high-producing Holsteins are more sensitive to ration quality. These are configured relative differences, not proof that one feed is cheapest on your map.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 19.1 Grain accepted by a trough but not eaten
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: F2M registers grain categories in some cattle troughs for Real-equivalent rations. Acceptance into storage does not mean Legacy will consume the new group.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: If 2000 L of maize is present but the cattle remain short of food, inspect Feed model. Supply a base feed the active rules actually consume rather than adding more maize. The UI marks these entries Not fed in legacy or similar.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 20. DM, ME, CP, NDF and peNDF
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: DM / Dry Matter: the dry feed mass containing nutrients after most water is excluded. ME / Metabolizable Energy: usable energy budget for maintenance, growth, pregnancy and milk. CP / Crude Protein: an approximate measure of protein supply for growth and production. NDF / Neutral Detergent Fibre: fiber and rumen-fill constraints. peNDF / Physically Effective NDF: effective roughage that constrains excessively concentrate-heavy rations. DM share: proportions by dry matter, not game liters. Intake: nutrients actually consumed and whether they meet requirements.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 20.1 Why 1000 L grass is not 1000 L TMR
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Fresh grass contains more water; hay is drier; TMR has its own density and dry-matter fraction. Real-equivalent converts liters into dry-matter kilograms using density and DM content, then calculates energy, protein and fiber.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Equal volumes therefore do not support a herd for equal periods. Examine DM shares, planned monthly liters and remaining supply rather than trough fill alone.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 20.2 Understanding resourceScale = 0.125
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: The default model keeps nutritional requirements unchanged but accounts for game feed resources at one eighth of their real-equivalent volume, to fit map yields, transport capacity and game pacing.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: This does not make biological feed conversion eight times better. It also does not guarantee one eighth of Legacy consumption: Legacy quantities are already game-scaled. Compare the actual breed, feed and growth state.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: This scale is for feed-resource conversion in this mode. It does not instruct you to divide water, straw, meat prices or milk output by eight.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 21. Ration controls [Opt-in]
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: A supported Real-equivalent pen offers Ration on Info (usually G; follow the actual binding).
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Feed for: Automatic, Finishing, Growth or Maintenance. Finishing generally targets commercial gain; Maintenance can be considered for animals not being actively finished, subject to their physiological needs.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Concentrate: Auto grain, No grain or an available grain. Having grain does not mean every animal needs it.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Concentrate share (DM): AUTO or 0-80% in 5% steps. This is a target, not an unconditional command.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Substitute when out: Allowed / Not allowed. Allow substitutions to keep supply going, or disable them when controlling ingredients precisely.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Preview: ingredient liters, DM shares, inventory, remaining time and energy coverage. Previewing does not consume feed.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Apply: saves the configuration; multiplayer changes become effective after server confirmation.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 21.1 Feeding objectives
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Automatic chooses an appropriate objective by animal class: bulls/steers generally favor FINISH, females GROW, while milk-dependent calves have separate arrangements.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Finishing aims to supply reasonable intake for sustained gain toward a suitable finished state; energy and financial costs can be higher.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Growth supports planned growth, physiological demands and moderate reserve recovery. It is not unlimited concentrate feeding.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Maintenance emphasizes body maintenance, basic metabolism and pregnancy rather than rapid gain. In high-producing cows, check actual milk and BCS particularly carefully.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: This is a pen-level target, not an advanced individual recipe editor for each animal.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 21.2 Why a 50% target may produce 30%
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Fibre limit: more effective roughage is required; add roughage or lower concentrate. Starch limit: starch/rapid fermentation constraint; reduce grain or change ingredients. Wheat limit: wheat share has reached its limit. Adapting: rumen adaptation is still limiting concentrate intake; increase gradually. No roughage: pure grain cannot substitute for a reasonable roughage base. Grain short / Feed short: replenish supplies and inspect substitution settings. Intake limit / Rumen full: intake or fiber-fill capacity is limiting; better nutrient density may help more than additional liters. Low protein: protein may limit gain or milk. Needs met: the current objective is satisfied; more concentrate may be unnecessary. Water short: restore water, especially for lactating animals.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Example: Target 50%, Now 20% (Adapting), Adapted 35% (Fibre limit). Intake starts at 20%, and even after adaptation the current ingredients may only allow 35%. The target has not been forgotten.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 21.3 The five preview columns
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Feed: ingredient name; confirm the pen can actually consume it. L/month: predicted game liters per month, useful for storage and transport planning. DM share: the ingredient's share of pen dry-matter intake. Stock: current inventory, which may be substantial but rapidly consumed. Lasts: estimated remaining supply; replenish the earliest shortage first.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Animal numbers, pregnancy/lactation, feed quality, weather, meadow supply and management changes alter the forecast. It is a prediction under present conditions, not a guaranteed future bill.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 22. Three additional individual readings
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: 22.1 DM / ME cover: 6.2 kg/d (85%). The first value is dry-matter intake per animal per model day; 85% is energy-demand or plan coverage, not 85% of required feed liters. Combine it with grain-limit reasons, stocks, water and BCS/Finish trends to identify the constraint.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 22.2 Grain DM / limit: 25% / Fibre limit means concentrates supply 25% of intake dry matter and effective fiber is limiting. It does not mean 25% of trough contents or 25 L per day.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 22.3 Finish estimate: ~2.4 mo predicts around 2.4 model/game months under current conditions. Gain too low means the estimated gain cannot support a reliable finish-time prediction; improve ration, health or growth conditions. Ready indicates the corresponding completion conditions are met; also read Slaughter.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: This is not a forecast of future beef prices or a guarantee of maximum profit in 2.4 months.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 23. Calves do not need milk until adulthood
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: 23.1 Hof Bergmann calf facilities [Map-specific]: the enabled calfRearing.xml rules manage milk-to-solid transition, with a reference weaning age of three months. Weaning and moving house are different events.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Approximate continuous age / maximum milk-demand share / maximum solid-feed share: Newborn: 100% / 10%. One month: 90% / 30%. Two months: 70% / 60%. Three months: 35% / 90%. Four months onward: 0% / 100%.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: These are request caps per calf, not trough-volume mixing instructions. The two columns need not sum to 100%. Actual intake depends on stocks and nutrients.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Young calves offered only hay/TMR without required milk can lose growth and health. Calves later in weaning offered only milk without solid feed can also be undernourished.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 23.2 Moving to group housing is not weaning
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Individual igloos mainly serve ages 0-1 months; group calf housing mainly ages 0-5 months. Moving at around two months can precede weaning.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Over-age animals are not automatically expelled. Warnings suggest suitable destinations, leaving the move to the player. Permission to remain does not mean the old pen is the best long-term housing.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 23.3 Calves grazing with their mothers
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Suckler calves and artificially reared calves follow different paths. In applicable ordinary cattle pens, Real-equivalent allows a calf to obtain milk from its own lactating dam. Calves receive priority; only remaining saleable milk may reach the tank.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: A missing/non-lactating dam can produce a warning and fallback. Do not count all milk from Angus, Hereford or other suckler cows as simultaneously available for sale. Nursing and sales compete for the same resource.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 24. Read milk, feeding and BCS together
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Lactation, dry periods and subsequent calving form a cycle. Age, breed, milk genetics, health, nutrition and reserves influence output.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Older discussions of Holstein 378 L/month do not describe this document's latest curve scale. The 11 October 2026 design increased some breed scales and bridged them to Real-equivalent energy requirements. Do not compare numbers from different versions as a simple production multiplier.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Check Lactating Yes/No, Milk output as a share of potential, BCS and its trend, ration/energy coverage, and actual monitored monthly production, tank contents and sales. Milk genetics are not liters.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Example: cow A has higher milk genetics but BCS 2.1 and only 70% realized output; cow B has slightly lower genetics but BCS 3.0 and adequate nutrition. B may be steadier in the short term. Improving A requires comparing additional feed costs with recovered milk and fertility value.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 25. A male and female do not guarantee offspring
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Breeding checks species, sex, minimum age, health, postpartum recovery, available males/semen, existing pregnancy and random conception. Condition also affects some species.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Under X months: below breeding age; good genetics do not bypass it. Recovers in X: postpartum recovery is incomplete. No suitable male: supply a qualifying male or arrange AI. Health below X: insufficient current health. Pregnant Yes: already pregnant; repeated mating does not increase litter size. Infertile: a special zero fertility coefficient prevents normal breeding.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Reproduction describes state/progress; Fertility genetics are inherited; BCS is an additional conception modifier. They are not one percentage.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 26. Pregnancy information
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Pregnant Yes confirms an existing pregnancy. Expecting records expected offspring; species differ in singles, twins and litters. Expected gives the estimated birth date. Father / Impregnated by can identify the sire or origin.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: The simulation handles progress, birth, inherited traits, birth weight and survival. Two expected offspring do not guarantee two survivors; health, disease, birth rules and space can change the result.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 26.1 Typical reference cycles: cattle about ten game months, usually one calf with occasional twins; pigs about four months with litters; sheep/goats about five months with singles/twins; horses about eleven months with few offspring. Chickens use a separate game breeding process, not exact real incubation time.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: These are explanatory references, not guarantees for every breed. Actual ages, gestation and fecundity follow subtype settings and the save. Map-added geese, ducks and rabbits may differ.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 27. AI and collecting semen from owned sires
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Artificial Insemination supports purchased semen. F2M also adds collection, storage and sale from owned sires: 1. Select an eligible, appropriately aged male. 2. Store collected semen in a dewar or other carrier, retaining sire identity and a genetic snapshot. 3. Inseminate an eligible female; success and maternal-state checks still apply. 4. Sell spare semen through the applicable interaction. The Hof Bergmann bull barn's native collection/packing chain is connected but not identical.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Semen value is not simply a bull's meat value. Breeding index, age, fertility and success affect quantity or price. Collection economics, live sire valuation and meat valuation are different systems. Live price divided by straw count is not a fixed semen-price formula.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 27.1 Choose matings for your purpose: dairy improvements prioritize milk and health rather than maximum beef frame; commercial calves require meat, frame/feed balance and a market; breeding-stock sales need maternal capacity, rearing time and buyers; avoid risky inherited-disease pairings.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 28. Three health concepts
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Current Health 0-100 changes with current care and conditions. Health Genetics 0-99 describes inherited tendencies for loss/recovery and resilience. Disease status tracks infection, treatment, recovery, immunity, vaccination or carriage.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: An animal with Health genetics 80 can fall to current Health 50% after prolonged water shortage. A genetically weaker animal can temporarily be at 100% when well cared for. Current state describes today; genetics describe tendency.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 28.1 Investigate edible feed, water, actual energy, illness and persistent underweight. Serious problems can cause losses when death/disease is enabled. Strong health genetics are not immunity from death. In Real-equivalent, prolonged inability to pay maintenance/pregnancy demands uses reserves and eventually harms health. A short deficit does not necessarily kill an animal in that hour.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 29. Diseases [Available by default; adjustable difficulty]
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Choose Off, Easy, Normal, Hard or Very Hard, and optionally disable individual diseases. Difficulty affects incidence, spread and some hidden-stage behavior.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Mastitis: lactating cattle/goats; threatens milk production. Foot and Mouth: cattle, pigs, sheep and others; wide spread and serious production losses. BRD: cattle, especially calves. PED: pigs, especially piglets; high early-life risk and altered slurry output. Footrot: cattle, sheep and goats; persistent production loss. Avian Flu LPAI: poultry; egg and health effects. Avian Flu HPAI: poultry; severe risk, potentially requiring culling. Pulpy Kidney: sheep/goats, especially young; treatment is not guaranteed. Colic: horses; potentially serious individual loss, unlike ordinary contagious herd disease. CVM: inherited in cattle, not contagious.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: This is an introduction, not a fully current list of symptoms, fees, courses, immunity lengths and eligible species. Use the disease dialog and current configuration.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 29.1 Hidden infection, symptoms and protection
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Hidden infection: at some higher difficulties an infected animal may have no visible symptoms/icon yet. Symptoms: production, health or sale eligibility can be affected; ordinary dealer/slaughter sale is usually blocked. Treatment: pay for a course; success can vary. Recovered immunity: temporary disease-specific protection. Vaccination: protection for a stated period; not available for all diseases and not treatment for an already infected animal. Inherited carriage: a CVM carrier may appear healthy but pass on risk; this differs from symptomatic contagious disease.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 29.2 Can sick animals be sold?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Symptomatic animals usually cannot enter ordinary dealer or slaughter transactions. Cull is a separate disposal action with a reduced recovery, around 33% of current value in inherited disease logic. It is not automatic accident-death compensation.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Current F2M removed the old automatic 33% sale-value return for accidental death. Voluntary disease culling and death from accidents, disease or age have different settlement rules.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 30. Accidents and natural losses
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Animal Death and Accident Chance are configurable. Low species/age-specific accident rates are evaluated per model month and multiplied by the setting. Changing one day per month to 28 does not simply multiply annual accidents by 28.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: The current background accident rate is not additionally increased by cold, disease, water or health. Disease and low health can cause harm through their own mechanisms.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Focus on controllable losses: newborns without feed, lactating cows without water, sick finished animals blocked from sale, and costly breeding purchases that do not fit your farm's purpose.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 31. Three kinds of animal value
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Live market value: what the current animal-sale rules pay, relevant to live sales and selection. Slaughter value: saleable meat times channel price, less slaughter and processing fees. Breeding/production potential: future milk, offspring and inherited improvements, relevant to retention and sire selection.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: An exceptional sire can sell far above its meat value. For commercial finished bulls without a breeding premium, compare live price with net processing return.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 32. Live weight, carcass and saleable product
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Standard-cattle reference: 600 kg live weight x 0.60 dressing = 360 kg carcass; x 0.75 saleable fraction = 270 kg saleable meat.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: This is a standard-animal baseline, not a guarantee for every 600 kg animal. Individual frame, breed, maturity, meat genetics and condition adjust output.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Species settings establish dressing and saleable fractions. Breed frame and slaughter references differ; buffalo should not be equated with Limousins. Light calves cannot produce full adult output. Meat genetics and overfat penalties matter. Age, orders, capacity, funds and facility state also determine whether delivery is possible.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 32.1 Other species: modeling references
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Cattle: 600 kg live -> 270 kg meat (0.60 x 0.75). Pigs: 125 kg -> 75 kg (0.80 x 0.75). Lambs: about 42.67 kg -> 19.2 kg, with breed variation. Chickens/common small poultry: 3 kg -> 1.89 kg, subject to species bridges.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: These are standard-animal product references, not monthly output or guaranteed meat per head. Check recipes, animal state and order results. Geese, ducks, rabbits and goats have separate rules rather than one approximate universal table.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 33. A player-friendly yield formula
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Saleable meat is approximately: standard species yield x individual/breed frame adjustment x live-weight maturity adjustment x breed carcass advantage x meat-genetics adjustment x applicable finishing-condition adjustment.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Frame uses bounded nonlinear factors, rather than letting adult target weight increase output without limit. A huge sire should not produce implausibly more meat than commercial cattle. Genetic effects have defined coefficient ranges, not direct extra kilograms.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 34. Public slaughterhouse and farm butcher [Hof Bergmann]
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Contract slaughter uses orders, delivery and fees and can reduce the work of running your own processing. The farm butcher is a player-operated production facility governed by recipes and operating rules.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: F2M aims for consistent product yield from the same animal through either path. Work, fees, orders and throughput differ. Order units, standard-animal equivalents and actual meat kilograms are distinct. One delivered order unit need not mean one kilogram.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: If output is still a fixed 1000 meat products per animal, inspect map/bridge versions. Early Hof Bergmann 1.5 Beta2 shared COW/MILKCOW input categories caused recipe matching problems; current code addresses that case, but release testing is still required.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 35. Slaughter fees
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: The current cattle reference in carcassYield.xml is a base fee of 100 per standard animal, plus 0.37 per actual saleable meat kg for cutting/packing. For 270 kg: 100 + 0.37 x 270 = 199.90 at the HARD reference scale.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: The base fee can scale with standard-animal equivalence for smaller/larger animals; cutting follows actual kilograms. It is not a universal fixed 200. Pigs/sheep have different rates; poultry/rabbits may use whole-product pricing. Economic-difficulty multipliers also apply.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 36. Why high meat prices can favor processing
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Live prices follow only part of meat-market movement; a common pass-through coefficient is about 0.6. High product prices can create more room for contract processing, while low prices may not cover the fee.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: The design also uses live-price floors and slaughter-net relationships to limit trivial arbitrage. Slaughter is not guaranteed to earn 12% more. Around 12% was a calibration reference for a representative animal over a seasonal year, not an order promise.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 36.1 Example calculation [Example]
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Assume meat sells at 8.4/kg and the animal yields 270 kg: Gross meat receipts = 270 x 8.4 = 2268.0. Processing fee = 100 + 270 x 0.37 = 199.9. Net processing receipts = 2068.1.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Against a live quote of 1900, that is about 168 more, before historic feed, purchase cost and pen occupancy. The 8.4 price is a calibration example, not a fixed price for every save, difficulty or selling point.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 36.2 A farm profit account
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Include purchase and transport costs; feed's opportunity cost; time occupying a pen; medication, monitoring, labor and losses; live receipts; slaughter and per-kg cutting fees; meat receipts; and differing supermarket, farm-shop or pub prices.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Finishing profit = final net sale receipts - total purchase cost - feed and care costs - corresponding time/facility costs. Buying at 1500 and selling at 1800 usually establishes a gross 300 spread, not net profit.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 37. Keeping or culling dairy cows
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: There is no universal sale age. Ask whether lower milk is a normal curve, a shortage or disease; whether BCS and reproductive age allow another pregnancy; whether milk/fertility/health genetics merit passing on; how current price compares with the next calf, remaining milk and eventual cull value; and whether a better replacement is available.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: The cattle valuation model includes remaining breeding and production economics. A genetically strong cow near peak lactation can be worth much more than an old cow valued mainly for meat.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 38. Breeds are more than names and colors
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: These are gameplay roles based on the current design, not an official real-world breed ranking.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Holstein: high milk and high dairy intake; dairy-focused, with male calves potentially reared separately for beef. Swiss Brown: dairy/beef dual purpose and substantial milk; retain health and milk traits in replacements. Angus: commercial beef and calf breeding; watch finish, meat genetics and sire value. Limousin: larger beef frame; support growth stages and use individual finish references. Hereford: grazing and conventional finishing; balance forage use with costs. Highland: slower growth and extensive forage; do not impose intensive commercial finishing ages. Water Buffalo: specialist animals and facilities; verify buffalo-milk channels and map compatibility.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Third-party breed packs use mappings, bridges or parameter tables. Not every added breed has the same verification level on every map.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 39. Store animals or breeding stock?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Dealer inventory uses purposes, not a uniform random spread across every age: weaned calves, replacement heifers, breeding-ready/in-calf heifers, first-calvers, young cows, store bulls and young sires. Purposes influence age, pregnancy/calving history and eligibility.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Weaned calf: lower weight/price and more control, but longer feed costs and risk. Replacement heifer: future herd capacity, not necessarily ready to breed now. In-calf heifer: less waiting for mating/pregnancy, usually a higher purchase cost. Store bull / Feeder: further finishing; compare cost per gain and eventual sale value. Young sire: breeding potential, fertility and inherited production, rather than meat alone.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Sources include dairies, suckler herds, rearers and breeders. Some breeds only occur at suitable sources. Extra map animals outside these rules may use inherited behavior.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 39.1 Budget / Standard / Premium are stock-quality and pricing tiers, not species or pure age groups. Premium still requires inspecting all individual traits. Standard is the default. Changing quality can regenerate inventory; keep conditions fixed and recorded when comparing trades.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 39.2 Buying from a dealer usually costs more than the animal's base live-sale value. Sale proceeds can include transport deductions, with differences between direct pen sale and trailer delivery. Slaughter is a separate chain. Buying and immediately slaughtering should not be assumed to offer reliable free profit; market, fees, floors and quality constraints oppose trivial arbitrage.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 40. Hof Bergmann housing roles [Map-specific]
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Admission rules consider age, sex, breed, castration and construction stage.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Calf igloos: mainly 0-1 months; consider group housing around two months. Calf rearing boxes A/B: eligible male/female and castrated calves, roughly 0-5 months, not males only. Bull barn: eligible intact males from about six months, including breeding uses; check the actual animal type. Dairy/cow barn: milk and storage, subject to breed/female rules. Mixed cow barn: females, some calves and steers; weaned calves from about three months can qualify. Manage breeding risks when males are present. Cattle pasture: seasonal grass resources, not guaranteed high-energy finishing all year. Highland pasture: a breed whitelist, not every cattle breed. Buffalo pasture: buffalo and specialist milk chains, matching type and map version.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: The enclosed MILKCOW dairy uses a separate map animal type. It does not automatically inherit all ordinary COW features. Real-equivalent labels it Milk cows: legacy. A Holstein female proxy in growth configuration does not establish identical feeding, breeding, housing and meat behavior.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 40.1 Admission is normally checked when buying/entering/moving. Growing beyond the pen's intended age produces guidance rather than automatic expulsion or deletion. The player or suitable automation must organize the next stage.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 40.2 Some calf houses, pastures and butcher buildings need construction stages completed. A building's presence on the map does not prove it can accept deliveries yet.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 41. Other species
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: 41.1 Pigs: organize breeding sows and commercial finishing batches. Large litters demand capacity and staged sales; not every finishing pig needs to remain for breeding. PIG v2 growth/Real-equivalent curves remain disabled in weightProfiles.xml. Some developmental nutrition logic targets growing commercial pigs, while nursing sows/newborns fall back. Do not advertise a complete released pig system.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 41.2 Sheep: existing reproduction, wool, genetics and meat economics are usable. Breeds differ in weight, growth, wool and price. The repository also contains dam milk, weaning, creep feeding, EUROP fat and ewe BCS work, but SHEEP enabled=false / S5_CALIBRATION_OFF means that deeper model is not default gameplay.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 41.3 Goats may share the SHEEP backend type, but milk, markets and parameters differ. Do not manage them for sheep wool. Specialized sheep S5 logic excludes goats.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 41.4 Poultry, rabbits and map additions have their own reproduction, output and slaughter references, sometimes through bridges. Egg production and meat/cull decisions differ. Maps may lack facilities/products. Cattle BCS, milk budgets and Finish scores do not automatically apply to chickens or rabbits.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 41.5 Horses depend on training and care. Horse Care can involve riding, cleaning and automatic maintenance; do not apply cattle slaughter or milk calculations.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 42. RL Menu tabs
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Manage / Info: individual state, weight, genetics, disease, pedigree, naming, monitoring and castration. Read details before deciding to sell. Buy: dealer purchases and receiving pens; inspect preview, admission rules and balance. Sell: server-rechecked sales; an old displayed value is not a locked quote. Move: own pens and some processing deliveries, subject to admission and capacity. Transfer: trailer loading/unloading, potentially with different transport accounting. Insemination / AI: semen selection/purchase and AI, still affected by success, state and sire genetics. Herdsman: daily automatic tasks; test small and inspect filters. Messages: births, pregnancy, trades, disease and rule/automation results. Settings: models, disease, dealer, filters and display; some settings are shared or permission-gated.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Tabs depend on entry context, multiplayer permissions and map support. A context without Settings does not mean the feature disappeared.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 43. Default shortcuts (rebindable)
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Right Shift + O: open RL Menu. R: enter mod management from the base-game animal page. X: mark. M: monitor. I: AI. C: castrate. D: disease dialog. N: rename. F: cycle saved filters. G: ration editor for supported pens.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Follow the actual prompts. Conflicts, versions, localization and custom bindings change keys. Actions also depend on sex, species, ownership and eligibility.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 44. Saved Filters
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Reusable conditions can find finishing candidates, older nonpregnant cows, strong breeding prospects, sick animals or weak replacements. Do not assume a direct Ready field exists; filter age/weight first and review Slaughter if necessary.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: AND / Match all requires every condition, for example male cattle, at least 18 months and Meat >=70. OR / Match any accepts any condition, for example age >=30 months or symptomatic disease.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Start with a temporary quick filter, then save suitable rules. Cycle applicable saved filters with F. Settings controls species scope and visibility on owned, dealer or all pages.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 44.1 Genetic conditions use display scores 0-99, not the underlying 1.75 coefficient. Age normally uses months, weight kg and health 0-100. Monitoring can gate precise health/weight matching for owned animals, so an unmonitored animal may not match Weight >500 even if it looks heavy.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 44.2 Quick filters are temporary browsing tools. Saved filters can work across contexts and drive Herdsman tasks. A price slider or another quick condition may have no equivalent saved field; conversion is not always lossless.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 45. Herdsman
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: The server runs configured daily tasks: Sell, Move, Buy, Castrate, Naming, AI and Horse Care. Define action, filter, pens, quantity, budget and enabled state.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 45.1 Order: Sell -> Move -> Buy -> Castrate -> Naming -> AI -> Horse Care. This allows selling to free capacity before buying, but broad sale filters can remove valuable breeding stock first. Begin with one pen, a small quantity and strict criteria; inspect messages before expanding.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 45.2 Common mistakes: no selected pens does not mean all pens; sex/age-only filters can sell breeding animals; full receiving pens block purchases; admission rules block moves; symptomatic animals may not sell; and old quotes are not final settlement. Check marks, genetics, selected pens, capacity, permissions, funds and server messages.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: The Herdsman has wages/management costs. It is not free transport or unlimited labor, and multiplayer tasks require suitable permissions.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 46. Important RL Settings
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Animal Death: On by default; losses can arise from disease, poor health, age and accidents. Accident Chance: default 1.0, multiplying a species/age baseline. 2.0 does not mean 2% per month. Diseases: default Normal, controlling disease-related difficulty. Choose Diseases: individual toggles can alter breeding risk and milk logic; decide about CVM early. Food Scale: default 1.0, scaling traditional feed consumption. Record changes during cost comparisons. Nutrition Model: default Legacy; Real-equivalent is opt-in and only qualifying pens switch. Max Dealer Animals: default 50; adjust for inventory scale and performance. Dealer Quality: default Standard; tiers affect expected quality/quotes. Keep fixed for market studies. Monitoring/display: information access and costs depend on settings and individual state. Saved Filters: player-created rules for management and automation.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Economic HARD/NORMAL/EASY is separate from disease Normal/Hard. Economic difficulty affects some products, live prices and fees; disease difficulty controls the disease model.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 47. Actual enablement at the documentation baseline
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Individual identity/pedigree: default. Genetics, reproduction, AI and disease: core features, some individually switchable. COW v2 growth: weightProfiles.xml enabled=true, still subject to applicability. COW reserves, Finish and BCS: bodyCondition.xml enabled=true for qualifying cattle. Cattle breeding cash-flow valuation: breedingValue.xml enabled=1. Hof Bergmann calf rearing: calfRearing.xml enabled=true plus map bridge. Real-equivalent: disabled by default in saves; opt-in with supported pens. SHEEP S5 milk/condition/lamb fat: enabled=false, calibration rather than default play. PIG new growth/nutrition: enabled=false, not a complete default replacement. Dealer v2 transaction backend: separate runtime switches and testing gates; ordinary players retain the current regular dealer. T02 recovery/transactions: OFF/SHADOW/TEST development switches, default off; not for unaccepted production saves. MILKCOW: separate map type without every ordinary COW feature.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Code may merge before calibration and live acceptance. A function, passing offline test or translated label alone does not prove a player is running that system.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 48. Files, versions and save compatibility
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: 1. Back up saves, especially valuable breeding herds, pregnancies, IDs and facilities. 2. Avoid enabling a second independent Realistic Livestock installation that rewrites the same objects/scripts. 3. Map-version changes require checking admission lists, public-slaughter inputs and production points. 4. Separate SellPrices changes are not synonymous with F2M. Feed, crop, milk and meat pricing alters opportunity costs and profits; record installed pricing mods. 5. Renaming does not complete migration. Some override paths retain modSettings/FS25_RealisticLivestockRM/ for compatibility; do not blindly replace every old name. 6. The multiplayer server rechecks transactions, reproduction, production, ration configuration and automation; stale client values are not authoritative.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 49. Advanced XML configuration
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: breedTraits.xml: breed growth, intake and forage use; errors distort feed conversion and pricing. weightProfiles.xml: age/weight curves and enablement; affects growth timing and save migration. bodyCondition.xml: reserves and allocation; affects milk, conception and meat together. feedProfiles.xml: DM, ME, protein and concentrates; affects intake, health and finishing. carcassYield.xml: dressing, saleability, fees and market linkage; errors can create fixed yields or arbitrage. breedingValue.xml: breeding-stock valuation and extreme premiums. calfRearing.xml: milk/solid transition; mistakes can prevent effective intake. dealerStock.xml: ages, purposes and sources; mistakes can remove breeds from stock.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Adult frame, finishing reference, meat quantity and live price are calibrated separately. Do not simply inflate targetWeight or set saleableRate to 1 for easy profit. Test the entire growth-feed-slaughter-price loop in a separate save before using overrides.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 50. Route A: low-input grazing beef
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: For players interested in pasture, suckler cows and store production. Choose suitable forage breeds and use Hof Bergmann grazing facilities.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Route: breeding cows -> mating/calving -> calves with dams or in calf housing -> weaning -> grazing/rearing -> further finishing, store sale or slaughter.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Watch maternal health genetics, reproduction and BCS; calf growth; seasonal grass; and late-stage gain versus feed cost. Avoid assuming pasture provides free rapid growth all year or holding cheap cattle to full adult weight while tying up pens.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 51. Route B: buying stores for intensive finishing
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Suitable for reliable TMR, silage and grain supplies and commercial turnover. 1. Select weaned or partly grown stores; record price, weight, age and meat genetics. 2. Check receiving-pen rules and enough feed for the expected cycle. 3. Use Finish weight rather than adult Target weight. 4. Record weight/Finish regularly; in Real-equivalent also inspect DM/ME cover, finish estimate and ration constraints. 5. At Ready, compare live sale and net processing. Sell when further expected value no longer covers the next month's feed and capital use.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Another month does not guarantee another profit. Initial weight, purchase spread and proximity to specification matter. An already fat purchase may have little profitable gain left.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 52. Route C: dairy and replacement breeding
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Buy healthy high-milk replacements and verify breeding/pregnancy status. Supply energy, protein and water to lactating cows, monitoring realized output. Some early-lactation reserve loss can be normal, but persistently low BCS jeopardizes the next pregnancy.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Improve milk traits through semen or suitable sires while considering CVM. Plan separate calf, weaning and replacement housing. Evaluate remaining breeding value before culling older, low-output or repeatedly unhealthy cows.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 53. Route D: beef breeding stock
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Use Overall only for initial screening; retained sires need strengths in the traits your buyers and herd need. An expensive sire requires enough females and breeding cycles to realize its genetic value.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Example: a four-bull commercial finishing unit does not necessarily need to pay for every trait at 90 just to obtain Meat 90. A long-term improvement program with forty breeding cows has a stronger reason to pay a sire premium.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: 54. Route E: staged sheep and pig businesses
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Sheep: begin with ewe reproduction, lamb sales, wool and ordinary meat economics. Introduce milk pools, creep feeding and EUROP explanations only when S5 is actually enabled by default.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Pigs: distinguish breeding sows from finishing batches. Do not expand the female herd indefinitely just to let every pig reproduce. Detailed staged rations and sow condition belong to the relevant new models once formally enabled.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q1. Why can a 1100 kg adult-target bull finish at 650 kg?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Adult frame and commercial finishing reference are different. Reaching around 95% of the finish reference, with appropriate age, condition and eligibility, can qualify it without growing into a fully mature sire.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q2. Is Finish 100 the best beef grade?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: No. Overfatness can reduce desirable saleable conversion. Roughly 65-80 is usually the preferred band, combined with weight and actual profitability.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q3. How does BCS 3.0 differ from Health 100%?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: BCS describes reserves; Health describes current health. A healthy animal can still be thin or fat.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q4. Why did an animal with Health genetics 95 become ill?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Genetic tendency is not immunity. Disease, water shortages, inadequate feed and other events can still occur.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q5. Does Overall 50 mean only 50% potential?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: No. It is a display mapping of mean genetic coefficients; neutral 1.0 is about display 50.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q6. Why does Fertility 80 still fail to conceive?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: It is a genetic score, not an 80% guaranteed conception roll. Eligibility, health, recovery, condition and random outcomes all matter.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q7. Does Fertility (BCS) 100% guarantee pregnancy?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: No. It only means current body condition adds no penalty.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q8. Does Milk output 80% mean 80% of milk was sold?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: No. It measures realized production against current potential. Read tanks and actual transactions for storage/sales.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q9. Why does a high-milk-genetics animal produce no milk?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: It may not be lactating, may be in unsuitable facilities, lack feed/water, have production-suppressing disease, or follow the map's separate MILKCOW rules.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q10. Why lose condition with a full trough?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: The active model may not consume that ingredient, nutrient density may be inadequate, or water/health may be limiting. Full inventory is not sufficient energy intake.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q11. Why is maize not eaten?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: The pen may be on Legacy, which does not consume the newly registered concentrate group. Read Feed model and Not fed in legacy.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q12. Why is a 60% concentrate target only 35% in practice?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: Fiber, starch, wheat limits, adaptation and inventory constrain actual intake.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q13. Does 6 kg/d mean six kilograms per game day?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: In Real-equivalent it is daily model dry matter. A game month currently represents thirty model days.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q14. Does enabling Real-equivalent switch every pen?
paragraph.heading: true

paragraph.text: No. Species, growth-model support, troughs, every resident animal and nursing conditions must qualify; otherwise a reason and Legacy fallback apply.
paragraph.heading: false

paragraph.text: Q15. Why does MILKCOW lack the full new ration?
paragraph.heading: true
